title: Streaming chunk reorder — cause analysis and provisional runbook
content:
Summary:

On 2026-10-30 23:12 UTC we observed a multi-region increase in tail streaming latency and a simultaneous small wave of client-observed truncated streams (partial payload then connection close). The signal showed elevated per-chunk reassembly times and reordering counts on a subset of edge multiplexer instances. Customer impact: degraded TTFB for streaming responses for ~2.5% of sessions (p95->p99 shift), and ~0.3% of sessions ended with an early stream termination (converted to a 5xx from the streaming proxy).

Why this doc exists:
- Capture an initial root-cause hypothesis that explains both the latency spike and the truncated-stream symptom
- Propose an actionable short-term runbook for on-call to detect and mitigate recurrence
- List follow-ups for engineering to harden reassembly and observability

High-level findings (evidence summary):
- Timeline of observed signals (UTC):
  - 2026-10-30 22:58: warning-level rise in chunk-reorder-rate in us-west-2 edge-tier (dashboards)
  - 2026-10-30 23:10: p95 streaming reassembly latency increases across multiple edges (us-west-2, eu-west-1)
  - 2026-10-30 23:12: customer SLO alert firing for hosted-api streaming TTFB in platform-monitor; support inbound tickets begin
  - 2026-10-30 23:18: small increase in proxy-initiated stream closes observed (application-logs)
  - 2026-10-30 23:40: mitigation performed (manual multiplexer drain + route shift) — signals recovered by 23:54
- Affected instances: 18 edge multiplexer replicas across 3 AZs in us-west-2, plus 6 in eu-west-1. Not all multiplexers in region were affected; pattern maps to a subset of behind-the-scene allocator groups.
content_continued:
Key telemetry details:
- metric: streaming.reassembly.chunk_reorder_count: spike from baseline ~0.02% -> 1.8% of chunks within 10 minutes on affected replicas
- metric: streaming.reassembly.latency_ms.p99: increased from 120ms -> 920ms on affected replicas
- logs: reassembly component logged 'out-of-order-chunk' at high frequency; many entries include sequence gaps of >3 chunks
- tcp metrics: no obvious network packet loss visible at edge host level; retransmit rates stable
- kernel queues: ephemeral socket backlog on a subset of multiplexers increased (somaxconn counters elevated)
- allocator traces: the allocator that assigns upstream inference connections shows a rare condition where connection handoff order differs from application-level sequence assignment (race between acceptor-thread and reassembly registration)

Root-cause hypothesis (single coherent narrative):
We believe a race between the acceptor/hand-off path and the stream reassembly registration led to temporary sequence-number assignment reordering on affected multiplexer replicas. Concretely: when a client opens multiple transport-level frames in quick succession, and the acceptor thread wakes and enqueues new connections while the reassembly registration path is concurrently reconciling shard ownership, the internal mapping between transport frames -> logical stream sequence can be assigned non-monotonically. The reassembly pipeline is tolerant of modest out-of-order delivery (we reorder in-memory), but the implementation uses a fixed-size fast-path buffer and, on detecting sequence gaps beyond N entries (N tuned low to conserve memory), it stalls waiting for missing chunks instead of tombstoning them or fetching from upstream. This results in reassembly stalls (increasing tail latency). In cases where upstream tears down or the allocator migrates the underlying connection during the stall, the reassembly code emits a truncated-stream and the proxy closes the session (client sees 5xx).

Why only a subset of replicas?
- The race requires a specific timing between acceptor wake-ups and registration reconciles; this timing correlates with multiplexers that were running a slightly older runtime build (rollout in progress) that had a hardened fast-path buffer size reduced. Those replicas hit the fast-path limit more easily.
- Traffic pattern: a small fraction of requests are very bursty (clients sending several small frames back-to-back), so only replicas serving that traffic shape see the spike.

Immediate actions taken during incident:
- 23:20 — SRE on-call shifted traffic away from affected allocator groups via temporary routing override (edge traffic rebalancer): reduced exposure within 6 minutes
- 23:28 — Orchestrated rolling restart of the 18 suspect multiplexer pods (graceful drain then restart)
- 23:40 — Deployed a defensive config: increase fast-path buffer threshold on all multiplexers in region (config override) to reduce stalls
- 23:54 — Metrics returned to baseline; alerts cleared at 00:05

Short-term runbook (provisional) — to be used if we detect similar patterns again:
1) Detection (SRE on-call)
   - Dashboard to check: streaming.reassembly.chunk_reorder_rate by region/instance, streaming.reassembly.latency_ms.p99, edge.ephemeral.socket_backlog
   - Pager triggers: chunk_reorder_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m OR streaming p99 > 400ms with correlated increase in proxy-close-rate
2) Triage steps
   - Identify affected allocator groups (SRE dashboard include allocator_id dimension)
   - If affected_count < 10% of replicas in region: perform targeted route override to divert traffic from allocator group (edge rebalancer UI, tag: allocator_id)
   - For severe region-wide: run global route shift away from region (use resilient fallback region) following standard cross-region failover playbook
3) Mitigation (fast)
   - Increase reassembly fast-path buffer threshold on affected replicas (config flag: REASSEMBLY_FASTPATH_THRESHOLD) via remote config (short-term)
   - If config change not possible: graceful drain -> restart affected multiplexer pods
   - Monitor chunk_reorder_rate and p99 after each mitigation step; allow 10 minutes stabilization window
4) Escalation
   - If mitigation doesn't bring p99 down in 20 minutes, escalate to Serving Runtime lead and Platform Networking lead; open Slack emergency channel and invite product-support for customer comms

Longer-term engineering follow-ups (owners + target dates):
- A: Fix race in acceptor vs reassembly registration so logical-sequence assignment is strictly monotonic (owner: Marcus Liu, target: 2026-12-10)
- B: Remove stall-on-gap behavior: implement bounded backfill + tombstone logic so reassembly does not block indefinitely waiting for missing chunks (owner: Priya Nair, target: 2027-01-07)
- C: Add canary config to test fast-path buffer sizes across small traffic slices before cluster-wide rollouts (owner: Ethan Brooks, target: 2026-12-01)
- D: Instrument new metrics: reassembly.sequence_gap_distribution, reassembly.tombstone_count, allocator.handoff-latency (owner: Sofia Ramos, target: 2026-11-20)
- E: Integrate a stream-health hook to surface truncated-stream events to the alerting plane (owner: SRE Infra, target: 2026-11-30)

Post-incident communication plan:
- Draft a short customer-facing note summarizing impact & mitigation (product-support): "We observed a small fraction of streaming sessions with increased latency; we mitigated by routing and config changes. A software fix and additional monitoring are in progress." (owner: product-ops, ETA: 2026-11-04)
- Internal postmortem (this doc -> final): add detailed timeline, logs, and PR links once the acceptor fix is merged (owner: Riley Chen, ETA: 2026-11-12)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did allocator handoff ordering expose itself only when combined with the fast-path buffer change? (hypothesis: reduced buffer reduces tolerance window — needs fuzz testing)
- Is there an upstream client pattern that can be nudged to reduce burstiness? (liaise with solutions-eng to surface to customers)

Quick checks for on-call when paged (cheat sheet):
- run: curl -s "${METRICS_API}/query?metric=streaming.reassembly.chunk_reorder_count&region=$REGION" | jq
- check running builds: kubectl get pods -l app=stream-multiplexer -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,IMAGE:.spec.containers[0].image
- if build mismatch: escalate to release-engineering to hold rollouts for suspected revision
- to drain a node safely: kubectl annotate pod <pod> "redwood/sre-drain=yes" && kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=45

Lessons learned (short):
- Small timing races can be amplified by micro-optimizations (buffer reductions) that reduce tolerance to natural network/traffic jitter
- Observability gaps: we lacked a sequence-gap metric and quick mapping from allocator -> multiplexer; adding those will shorten TTR on future incidents
- Defensive default behavior should favor forward progress (tombstoning/backfill) over indefinite stalls even if it means slightly higher reassembly smoothing later

Appendix (links to evidence):
- allocator trace samples: logs/alloc-trace/us-west-2/allocator-77/2026-10-30-23xx (internal link)
- streaming reassembly error log tail: logs/streaming/reassembly/2026-10-30
- rolling restart commands (operator runbook): runbook/ops/streaming-multiplexer-drain-v1

Action items (explicit):
- [ ] Create SLO-impact summary for exec (owner: Riley Chen, due: 2026-11-05)
- [ ] Start engineering RFC for acceptor fix (owner: Marcus Liu, due: 2026-11-12)
- [ ] Add new observability panels + alert rules (owner: Sofia Ramos, due: 2026-11-20)
- [ ] Implement bounded backfill in reassembly (owner: Priya Nair, due: 2027-01-07)

If you're on-call and see this pattern, follow the short-term runbook above and ping #sre-urgent and the owners listed in follow-ups.
